questions.prompt: InfoNCE with N=2: z1=z1'=(1,0), z2=z2'=(0,1), tau=1. What is the loss? (decimal, tolerance 0.001)
If an encoder collapses and maps every input to the same vector, what is the InfoNCE loss for a batch of N=64 (any tau)? (decimal, tolerance 0.001)
questions.explanation: All logits equal, so each softmax is 1/64 and the loss is ln 64=4.159.

questions.prompt: Why do contrastive methods with an InfoNCE-type loss need negatives (or another collapse-prevention mechanism)?
options: Without them, mapping all inputs to one point makes the two views trivially agree
They reduce the batch size that is needed, so that each training step is cheaper
Negatives make the gradients larger, which in turn speeds up the optimisation
Negatives provide the class labels that the contrastive loss needs in order to learn
questions.explanation: Agreement alone is minimized by a constant encoder; negatives make that solution cost log N.

questions.prompt: BERT-style masking selects 15% of a 200-token sequence. How many tokens are selected for prediction? (integer, tolerance 0.01)
In masked prediction, on which positions is the loss usually computed?
questions.explanation: Computing the loss on visible tokens rewards copying; the task is to infer hidden content.

questions.prompt: You train a contrastive model on signals whose downstream label is the signal's dominant frequency. Which augmentation is dangerous?
options: Flipping the sign of the signal, so that it is inverted in amplitude
Adding small Gaussian noise with a low amplitude to each sample
Circular time shift of the signal by a random number of samples
questions.explanation: Stretching changes the frequency, which is the label itself; the others keep it.

questions.prompt: You will pretrain with contrastive learning on a robot's camera frames to later recognise object categories. Describe how you would choose and validate the augmentations, and what failure you would look for.
rubric: Lists augmentations tied to nuisance factors (crop, lighting, blur) and excludes ones that change the label (e.g. colour jitter if colour identifies the class, flips if handedness matters).
Validates with a probe set of known labels (preserved fraction) and a downstream linear probe versus raw baseline over several seeds.
Looks for shortcuts, false negatives from near-duplicate frames, and collapse (loss stuck at log N).
questions.explanation: Rubric-guided: compare your answer with each rubric point; this question is not automatically graded.
